''tron'', ''tro'' = Sp. ''trono'' = Pg. ''throno'' = It. ''trono'', < L. ''thronus'', < Gr. θρόνος, a seat, chair, throne, < θράειν, set, aor. mid. θρήσασθαι, sit.] 1. A chair of state; a seat occupied by a sovereign, bishop, or other exalted personage on occasions of state. {{smaller|The throne is now usually a decorated arm-chair, not necessarily of remarkable}} richness, and seldom of great size, but usually raised on a dais of one or two steps, and covered with an ornamental canopy. Ancient and Oriental thrones are described and represented as very elaborate, made in part of precious materials, or raised very high with different substructures, and supported on figures of beasts or men. [[File:century v08 p0117 c1f1.png|center|360px]] {{c|Oriental Throne of marble, with gilded carvings, in the palace at Teherân, Persia.}} {{smaller block|“O, myghty God,” quod Pandarus, “in ''trone.''” {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1086.}}}} {{smaller block|Twelve ''thrones'' were designed for them, and a promise made of their enthronization. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 262.}}}} {{smaller block|After considerable delay, the King received the Oxford and Cambridge addresses on the ''throne'', which (having only one ''throne'' between them) he then abdicated for the Queen to seat herself on and receive them too. {{right|''Greville'', Memoirs, July 20, 1830.}}}} 2. Sovereign power and dignity; also, the wielder of that power; also, episcopal authority or rank; often with the definite article. {{smaller block|Thy ''throne'', O God, is for ever and ever. {{right|Ps. xlv. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|Fond Tyrant, I'll depose thee from thy ''Throne.'' {{right|''Cowley'', The Mistress, Usurpation.}}}} {{smaller block|Hugh III., the new king, had the advantage of acquiring ''the throne'' when he had age and experience to fill it: and he reigned fourteen years. {{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 178.}}}} 3. ''pl.'' The third order of angels in the first triad of the celestial hierarchy. See ''celestial hierarchy'', under ''hierarchy''. {{smaller block|The mighty regencies Of seraphim, and potentates, and ''thrones'', In their triple degrees. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 749.}}}} {{smaller|'''Bishop's throne.''' See ''bishop'' and ''cathedra.''—'''Speech from the throne.''' See ''speech.''}} '''throne''' (thrōn), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''throned'', ppr. ''throning''. [< ME. ''thronen'', ''troner''; < ''throne'', ''n.'' Cf. ''enthrone'', ''thronize.''] I. ''trans.'' 1. To set on a throne; enthrone. {{smaller block|The firste Feste of the Ydole is whan he is first put in to hire Temple and ''throned.'' {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 232.}}}} {{smaller block|As on the finger of a ''throned'' queen The basest jewel will be well esteem'd. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xcvi.}}}} 2. To set as on a throne; set in an exalted position; exalt. {{smaller block|''Throned'' In the bosom of bliss. {{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 596.}}}} II. ''intrans.'' To sit on a throne; sit in state as a sovereign. [Rare.] {{smaller block|He wants nothing of a god but eternity and a heaven to ''throne'' in. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 4. 26.}}}} {{smaller block|Every one here is magnificent, but the great Veronese is the most magnificent of all. He swims before you in a silver cloud; he ''thrones'' in an eternal morning. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'' Portraits of Places, p. 29.}}}} '''throneless''' (thrōn′les), ''a.'' [< ''throne'' + ''-less.''] Without a throne, especially in the sense of having been deprived of a throne; deposed. {{smaller block|Must she too bend, must she too share Thy late repentance, long despair, Thou ''throneless'' Homicide? {{right|''Byron'', Ode to Napoleon.}}}} '''throng'''1 (thrông), ''n.'' [< ME. ''throng, thrang,'' < AS. ''gethrang'' = D. ''drang'' = MHG. ''dranc,'' G. ''drang,'' throng, crowd, pressure (cf. OHG. ''gidrengi,'' MHG. ''gedrenge,'' G. ''gedränge,'' thronging, pressure, throng, crowd, tumult), = Icel. ''thröng,'' throng, crowd; cf. Sw. ''trång'' = Dan. ''trang,'' throng, = Goth. *''thraihns,'' crowd, quantity (in ''faihuthraihns,'' riches); < AS. ''thringan'' (pret. ''thrang''), press: see ''thring.'' Cf. ''throng''2.] 1. A crowd or great concourse of people; a multitude, great in proportion to the space it occupies or can occupy. {{smaller block|A thral thryȝt in the ''throng'' unthryuandely clothed, Ne no festiual frok, but fyled with werkkez. {{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 133.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''throng'' that follows Cæsar at the heels . . . Will crowd a feeble man almost to death. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 4. 34.}}}} {{smaller block|Now had the ''Throng'' of People stopt the Way. {{right|''Congreve'', Iliad.}}}} 2. A great number: as, the heavenly ''throng.'' {{smaller block|Not to know me argues yourselves unknown, The lowest of your ''throng.'' {{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 831.}}}} {{smaller block|O'er the green a festal ''throng'' Gambols in fantastic trim! {{right|''Cunningham'', A Landscape, ii. 5.}}}} '''3.''' A busy period, great press of business, or the time when business is most active: as, the ''throng'' of the harvest; he called just in the ''throng''. [Scotch.] = '''Syn.''' {{smaller|1. ''Crowd'', etc. See ''multitude''.}} '''throng1''' (thrông), ''v.'' [< ''throng''1, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To come (or go) in multitudes; press eagerly in crowds; crowd. {{smaller block|Menelay with his men meuyt in swithe, Thre thousaund full thro ''thrang'' into batell. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8283.}}}} {{smaller block|I have seen the dumb men ''throng'' to see him. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 1. 278.}}}} {{smaller block|The peasantry . . . ''thronging'' tranquilly along the green lanes to church. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 88.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To crowd or press; press unduly upon, as a crowd or multitude of people anxious to view something. {{smaller block|Much people followed him, and ''thronged'' him. {{right|Mark v. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|This foolish prophesie, That, vnlesse ''throngd'' to death, thou ne're shalt die; And therfore neither vnto church nor faire Nor any publicke meeting darst repaire. {{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 69.}}}} {{smaller block|Yet if, said he, I ''throng'' my Darling with this massy store, 'Twill to a Burden swell my Courtesy. {{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iii. 25.}}}} '''2.''' To crowd into; fill as or as with a crowd. {{smaller block|''Throng'' our large temples with the shows of peace, And not our streets with war! {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 3. 36.}} When more and more the people ''throng''
The chairs and thrones of civil power. {{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xxi.}}}} {{smaller block|On the ''thronged'' quays she watched the ships come in. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 254.}}}} 3†. To fill or stuff. {{smaller block|A man ''throng'd'' up with cold; my veins are chill,
And have no more of life than may suffice
To give my tongue that heat to ask your help. {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 1. 77.}}}} '''throng'''2 (thrông), ''a.'' [Sc. also ''thrang''; < ME. *''thrang'', *''throng'', < Icel. ''thröngr'', ''thraungr'', ''thrængr'' = Dan. ''trang'', narrow, close, tight, crowded, thronged; from the root of ''throng''1, ''thring''.] 1. Thickly crowded or set close together; thronged; crowded. {{smaller block|They have four hospitals, so big, so wide, so ample, and so large that they may seem four little towns, which were devised of that bigness, partly to the intent the sick, be they never so many in number, should not lie too ''throng'' or strait, and therefore uneasily and incommodiously. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|Lancers are riding as ''throng'' . . . as leaves. {{right|''Scott.''}}}} {{smaller block|Ay, I'm told 'Tis a ''throng'' place now. {{right|''J. W. Palmer'', After his Kind, p. 52.}}}} 2. Much occupied or engaged; busy. {{smaller block|In these times great men, yea and men of justice, are as ''throng'' as ever in pulling down houses, and setting up hedges. ''Sanderson's Sermons'' (1689), p. 113. (''Halliwell.'')}} [Obsolete or prov. Eng. and Scotch in both uses.] '''throng'''3†. Preterit of ''thring''. '''throngful''' (thrông′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''throng''1 + ''-ful''.] Filled by a throng; crowded; thronged. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The ''throngful'' street grew foul with death. ''Whittier'', The Female Martyr.}} '''throngly''' (thrông′li), ''adv.'' [< ''throng''2 + ''-ly''2.] In crowds, multitudes, or great quantities. ''Dr. H. More'', Philosophic Cabbala, ii. § 7. [Obsolete or provincial.] '''thronize†''' (thrō′nīz), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''tronysen''; by apheresis from ''enthronize''.] To enthrone. {{smaller block|By meane whereof he was there chosen pope about the vii. day of May, and ''tronysed'' in the sayd moneth of May. {{right|''Fabyan'', Chron., an. 1343.}}}} '''thrope†''', ''n.'' [ME., < AS. ''thrōp'', a village: see ''thorp''.] A thorp; a village. ''Piers Plowman'' (A), ii. 47. '''thropple''' (throp′l), ''n.'' [Also ''thrapple''; prob. a reduction of ''throat-boll'', < ME. ''throtebole'', < AS. ''throtbolla'', windpipe: see ''throat-boll''.] The throttle or windpipe. '''thropple''' (throp′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''throppled'', ppr. ''throppling''. [< ''thropple'', ''n.''] To throttle; strangle. [Prov. Eng.] '''Throscidæ''' (thros′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Throscus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of serricorn beetles, allied to the ''Buprestidæ'', ''Elateridæ'', and ''Eucnemidæ''. {{smaller|It differs from the first in having the ventral segments free, from the second in having the prothorax firmly articulated, and from the third by a different construction of the anterior coxal cavities. The family comprises 6 genera and rather more than 100 species, of which 3 genera and 17 species are found in the United States.}} '''Throscus''' (thros′kus), ''n.'' [NL. (Latreille, 1796), < Gr. θρῴσκειν, leap upon.] A genus of small serricorn beetles, typical of the family ''Throscidæ''. {{smaller|They have a three-jointed antennal club and tarsal grooves in the metasternum, and resemble click-beetles.
